answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the end of The Unnamable in Beckett’s own English version, published in 1958. It is the novel’s speaking voice, not a biographical remark; the English ending also revises the earlier French text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Published 1953; the endings should not be treated as identical

source.excerpt: I can't go on, I'll go on.
trail: The publisher Faber ↗ quotes the exact ending under the novel’s name.
Sam Slote’s Trinity essay ↗ explains the added English clause and its later effect on the French text.
source.rightsHolder: Samuel Beckett’s estate / Grove Press and the relevant English publishers
source.rightsNote: These are words from Beckett’s 1958 English self-translation of a modern novel. Both the original and this English version are treated as in copyright; only the short ending is reproduced for identification and discussion.

author.name: Samuel Beckett
author.heading: About Samuel Beckett
author.bio: Samuel Beckett wrote fiction and drama in both English and French, often translating and revising his own work between the two languages. His sparse settings and restless voices examine what remains when ordinary explanations and consolations stop working.

cite.sourceCitation: Beckett, Samuel. The Unnamable. Translated from the French by the author. New York: Grove Press, 1958. Ending corroborated by Faber’s publisher article “Back to Beckett.”
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘I can't go on, I'll go on’?” Last verified 9 Nov 2026.

copyAttribution: Samuel Beckett, The Unnamable, his English self-translation (1958), ending; words of the novel’s voice, not a personal interview remark.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The novel is carried by an unstable speaking voice that tries to account for itself and cannot finish doing so. Its ending holds inability and continuation together; Trinity scholarship notes that Beckett introduced the crucial inability clause while remaking the French text in English.

schema.claimReviewed: Samuel Beckett wrote the quoted ending in his English version of The Unnamable.
schema.faqAnswer: Yes. These are the concluding words of Beckett’s English self-translation of The Unnamable, published in 1958; they are spoken by the novel’s voice.
schema.verdictNote: The English wording is from the 1958 self-translation, not the first French edition.
